Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, in a prominent interview on Fox News on October 21, reiterated his long-standing position since November 2024 that he is open to freezing the current frontline in Ukraine to achieve an immediate ceasefire. Zelensky stated that he is open to accepting freezing the current frontline in Ukraine, which he also referred to as a ceasefire, and noted that Ukraine will ask for security guarantees from the US President Donald Trump and Europe after the ceasefire.[1] Some sources inaccurately presented Zelensky’s October 21 Fox News statement as a new Ukrainian concession despite Zelensky long offering this concession since 2024. Zelensky first publicly spoke about a ceasefire deal that would include de facto Russian control of Ukrainian territories without de jure recognition on November 29, 2024, and has since reiterated his openness to an immediate ceasefire.[2] Zelensky has repeatedly presented various ceasefires and peace proposals, which the Russian officials have continuously rejected and have not yet offered any meaningful concessions toward peace negotiations.[3]
Senior Kremlin officials reiterated Russia’s long-standing unwillingness to engage in any meaningful peace negotiations while attempting to present Ukraine and Europe as the main obstacles to peace in Ukraine.
Russian Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov provided his commentary following the October 21 meeting between US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St.
Petersburg.
[4] Ushakov stated that Witkoff briefed Putin on the Ukrainian and European peace proposals from Witkoff’s meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders in Oslo, Norway, on October 20, and Putin noted that those proposals have “little that was useful” in resolving the war in Ukraine.
Ushakov separately told Kremlin journalist Pavel Zarubin on October 21 that Russia “is not completely satisfied” with the “nuances” in European behavior.
[5] Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov claimed on October 21 that Russia’s position on an energy ceasefire with Ukraine has not changed and added that Russia “needs peace, not a ceasefire.
”[6] Russian State Duma International Affairs Committee member Denis Kravchenko claimed on October 21 that progress on resolving the war in Ukraine is possible but only if Russia’s “fundamental demands are met.
”[7] The Kremlin officials’ October 21 statements effectively rejected Ukraine’s and Europe’s peace proposals by labeling them as insufficient, indicating Russia’s intransigence in its war objectives and continued unwillingness to accept Zelensky‘s concessions.
The Kremlin officials continue reiterating the Kremlin’s long-standing narrative that Ukrainian and European leaders are the main obstacles to peace, despite Russia’s continuous rejections of Ukrainian and European ceasefire and peace proposals on any terms that fall short of fulfilling Russia’s goals of Ukraine’s complete capitulation despite the fact that the Russian military is unable to achieve those goals on the battlefield.
[8]
The Kremlin is attempting to negotiate under the false assumption that Russia holds the strategic initiative on the battlefield in Ukraine, despite ample evidence to the contrary. Ushakov claimed that Putin presented Witkoff with an “objective picture” of the frontline situation, where Russian forces have “complete strategic initiative.”[9] Ushakov further claimed that Russian forces are conducting a “relentless offensive” in all key areas of the frontline. Official Russian claims of Russian successes do not reflect the current battlefield realities, however, and are reflective of the pervasive culture of lying within the Russian military. Russian high-ranking military commanders also routinely present exaggerated Russian advances as part of Russia’s systematic cognitive warfare effort to portray Russian forces as making sweeping advances and Ukrainian defenses as collapsing.[10]
Russia is failing to achieve its battlefield objectives in reality, however, and Ukrainian counteroffensive operations have operationally defeated the planned Russian offensive to complete the seizure of Donetsk Oblast – Putin’s self-defined objective since 2022.
[11] ISW has observed evidence to assess that Ukrainian forces have liberated about 1,080 square kilometers of territory since January 1, 2026.
ISW has observed evidence to assess that Russian forces have net gained about 73 square kilometers since January 1, 2026, and suffered a net loss of about 73 square kilometers since September 1, 2026.
Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi in the Lyman direction defeated the northern pincer of Russia’s planned encirclement of Donetsk Oblast and liberated at least 277 square kilometers, continuing to generate cascading effects for Russian offensive operations in neighboring sectors.
[12] Ukraine has proven its ability to contest the operational initiative and disrupt Russian offensive plans on numerous occasions throughout 2026 and will likely be able to continue to do so in the coming months, assuming continued Western military support, intelligence sharing, and unimpeded access to Starlink and Starshield communications technologies.
Putin has set no fewer than 16 deadlines for the seizure of Donetsk Oblast since 2022 and Russian forces have failed to meet every single one.
[13] Putin’s battlefield perceptions remain divorced from the reality of Ukraine’s defensive abilities, Russia’s own degraded offensive capabilities, and the difficult and expansive terrain that Russian forces must still fight through to achieve Putin’s strategic goal in Donetsk Oblast.
Pro-war Russian sources continue to complain about how official Russian reports are deeply exaggerated and are not representative of battlefield reality.
[14]
Putin claimed that the first Russian fuel tanker carrying 40,000 tons of diesel will depart from Russia to the United States in two to three days and noted that other shipments will follow.[15] Russian Deputy Prime Minister and Economic Minister Alexander Novak also claimed that the first diesel shipment will depart on October 22, and that the United States and Russia are in the final stages of signing diesel contracts.[16] The US decision to import Russian diesel represents a unilateral concession in the US negotiating posture to Russia when Russia has offered no substantive concession to the US in return. The sale also primarily benefits Russia by providing the Kremlin with additional funding to protract the war in Ukraine while offering the US no significant price relief.[17]
Russia released US citizen Stephen Hubbard during Witkoff’s visit to St. Petersburg on October 21.[18] Russian authorities imprisoned Hubbard on October 7, 2024, for allegedly serving in the Ukrainian Armed Forces (which Russian authorities criminally charged Hubbard for) and sentenced him in 2024 to seven years in prison during closed court proceedings.
The United States, Ukraine, and Russia will likely hold trilateral peace negotiations around November 10. Ushakov claimed on October 21 that Putin told Witkoff that Russia is “in principle” ready to resume trilateral negotiations between Russia, Ukraine, and the United States around November 10 and suggested that such negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.[19] The United States, Ukraine, and Russia last held trilateral negotiations in February 2026.[20]

- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, in a prominent interview on Fox News on October 21, reiterated his long-standing position since November 2024 that he is open to freezing the current frontline in Ukraine to achieve an immediate ceasefire.
- Senior Kremlin officials reiterated Russia’s long-standing unwillingness to engage in any meaningful peace negotiations while attempting to present Ukraine and Europe as the main obstacles to peace in Ukraine.
- The Kremlin is attempting to negotiate under the false assumption that Russia holds the strategic initiative on the battlefield in Ukraine, despite ample evidence to the contrary.
- The United States, Ukraine, and Russia will likely hold trilateral peace negotiations around November 10.
- Russian forces recently advanced south of Dobropillya.
- Russian forces launched an unspecified number of Iskander-K cruise missiles and 186 drones and loitering munitions against Ukraine overnight on October 20 to 21.

articles.summary: Trump’s Russian Diesel Decision Weakened Pressure for Ukraine Ceasefire, Czech President Warns  UNITED24 Media
articles.full_text:
A ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine had been “quite close” before US President Donald Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel, undermining peace efforts, Czech President Petr Pavel stated on October 22.
This was reported by POLITICO on October 22, citing Pavel's interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters' Network.
Pavel argued that coordinated US and European sanctions targeting Russian oil, oligarchs, and other industries had placed Moscow under significant economic pressure. Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports gave the Kremlin "time to breathe" and weakened incentives to negotiate a ceasefire.
“It will be much harder now,” Pavel warned, describing the consequences of Washington's agreement with Moscow.
According to the Czech president, the agreement gave Russia “a new hope” that it could bypass Ukraine and European governments while pursuing direct negotiations with Washington and potentially Beijing.
Pavel warned that such an arrangement would allow Moscow to pursue its objectives without accounting for European security interests. He described this possibility as “clearly against our interest in Europe.”
The Czech president also addressed Trump's approach to the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin. Pavel suggested that Trump was attracted to Putin's exercise of authority and viewed international relations primarily through the lens of the United States' economic interests.
Rather than seeing Russia's invasion of Ukraine as a confrontation between democracy and authoritarianism, Trump appeared to approach the war through the potential economic benefits of negotiations, Pavel argued.
Pavel also defended Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy against criticism over the stalled diplomatic process.
“It was not Ukraine who attacked Russia,” Pavel emphasized, rejecting suggestions that Kyiv bore responsibility for the war.
Pavel acknowledged that European countries might eventually resume purchases of Russian oil. However, he emphasized that such cooperation would only become acceptable once Russia demonstrated respect for other countries' sovereignty and internationally recognized borders.
Washington's easing of pressure on Moscow has extended beyond fuel. Trump also blocked a package of Russia sanctions, approved by Congress and signed into law in September, just two days before it was due to take effect.
The 60-day suspension was framed as an effort to keep Russia at the negotiating table, and Moscow welcomed the move. Zelenskyy has warned that recent US decisions, including delayed Patriot deliveries, Starlink restrictions, and interruptions in intelligence sharing, appear to be pushing Kyiv toward capitulation.

articles.summary: Armenian export growth to EU deemed speculative amid trade rerouting  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Forecasts suggesting a sustained boom in Armenian exports to the European Union are fundamentally speculative, according to a new analysis by the Eurasian Rating Agency, which points to structural instabilities and the rerouting of trade through Belarus.
The October 22 research report challenges the narrative of Armenia's successful economic pivot toward Western markets, revealing that recent export spikes mask a deeper reliance on intermediate trade partners to bypass political complications with Russia. The findings highlight the vulnerabilities of landlocked economies navigating complex sanctions regimes and regional geopolitical fractures.
Statistical Anomalies and Supply Chain Distortions
The Eurasian Rating Agency's assessment directly contradicts optimistic projections that have circulated among Western policymakers and international financial institutions over the past two years. According to the research published on October 22, the apparent growth in Armenian exports to EU member states in 2025, when compared to 2024 figures, is "unstable by nature." When evaluated over a broader two-year interval, the data actually indicates a decrease in direct trade volumes. The agency concludes that any economic forecasts relying on the extrapolation of this recent, short-term growth are inherently speculative and fail to account for the underlying structural distortions in the region's supply chains.
At the heart of the agency's skepticism is the complex web of parallel imports and re-export mechanisms that have defined Eurasian trade since the imposition of sweeping Western sanctions on Moscow in 2022. The research notes a distinct divergence in bilateral trade flows: while direct supplies to Russia have declined amid ongoing political complications and logistical hurdles, exports to Belarus have simultaneously surged. The agency's analysts assume that a significant portion of Armenian producers are utilizing Belarus as an intermediate trade partner. Goods are ostensibly shipped to Minsk, only to be rerouted into the Russian market, a practice that has become commonplace across the Caucasus and Central Asia.
Trade Flow Anomalies
- EU Exports: Recent short-term growth is deemed statistically unstable and speculative over a two-year horizon.
- Belarus Corridor: Surging supplies to Minsk indicate the use of intermediate partners to bypass political friction with Russia.
- Cost Penalties: Rerouting through third countries inflates logistics costs and erodes the global competitiveness of Armenian goods.
The Cost of Parallel Trade Networks
This rerouting strategy carries severe economic penalties for Armenian businesses. By inserting an additional jurisdiction into the supply chain, producers incur compounded transit costs, customs fees, and intermediary margins. The Eurasian Rating Agency warns that this artificial elongation of the supply chain ultimately results in higher end-user costs and significantly reduces the global competitiveness of Armenian products. Rather than achieving genuine market diversification, these firms remain tethered to their traditional Russian consumer base, merely adopting a more expensive and legally opaque method of delivery to circumvent political friction and secondary sanctions risks.
The findings arrive at a critical juncture for macroeconomic strategy. Over the past eighteen months, the administration in Yerevan has aggressively pursued closer integration with European institutions, signaling a desire to reduce its historical economic dependence on the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). This diplomatic pivot has included discussions regarding access to the EU's single market for specific goods and increased technical assistance from Brussels. However, the physical reality of Armenia's geography—it is a landlocked nation bordered by Turkey, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Iran—severely limits its direct trade corridors with Europe. The reliance on the Georgian Black Sea ports or the Iranian north-south corridor remains fraught with logistical bottlenecks and geopolitical vulnerabilities.
Structural Limits of Statistical Diversification
The agency's report underscores a vital distinction between statistical trade diversification and genuine structural decoupling. While headline customs data might show an increase in goods registered for European destinations, the physical flow of commodities often tells a different story. International auditors and trade monitors have repeatedly flagged the Caucasus as a primary node for sanctions evasion, where dual-use goods and restricted technologies flow eastward under the guise of regional commerce. By highlighting the speculative nature of the export boom, the agency is cautioning investors and credit markets against misinterpreting customs anomalies as evidence of a successful, sustainable economic reorientation.
Moving forward, the sustainability of the export sector will depend less on diplomatic declarations in Brussels and more on the resolution of regional transit blockades. Furthermore, the reliance on Belarus as a conduit introduces significant currency and settlement risks. Transactions routed through Minsk are increasingly subject to the financial isolation of the Belarusian banking sector, complicating repatriation of profits for exporters. This financial friction further erodes the margins of small and medium enterprises attempting to navigate the fractured Eurasian market, proving that geographic and political realities cannot be easily overwritten by optimistic trade forecasts.

The Kremlin’s seeming interest in negotiations aims not to end the war in Ukraine but rather to secure economic concessions from the United States such that Russia can continue funding its war. Various Russian officials tried to present the October 21 meeting between US Special Representative to the Middle East Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin as evidence that Russia is willing to engage in meaningful negotiations to end the war while simultaneously attempting to extract economic concessions from the United States so that Russia can continue funding the war.[1] Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) CEO Kirill Dmitriev, for example, claimed on October 21 that Witkoff and Putin used the October 21 meeting to agree to expand Russian-US economic cooperation and to “continue communicating.”[2] A Kremlin domestic policy official told Russian opposition source Verstka that the Kremlin does not expect negotiations to resolve the war in Ukraine but that Russian officials hope to extract economic concessions, which could boost Russia’s budget and give Russia a military advantage.[3]
Other Russian officials meanwhile demonstrated Russia’s unwillingness to make any meaningful concessions toward ending the war in Ukraine. Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stated on October 22 that Putin did not present any Russian peace proposal to Witkoff during their meeting and that Putin has not considered the composition of a potential Russian delegation for a future Russia-US-Ukraine trilateral meeting.[4] Russian State Duma deputies expressed skepticism on October 21 and 22 that negotiations could end the war and reiterated claims that freezing the current frontlines would be detrimental to Russia’s own efforts to end the war.[5] A source close to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) told Verstka on October 22 that the Kremlin has been working for over 1.5 years to try to sway the Trump administration to Russia’s side and that the Kremlin’s current negotiation efforts are emphasizing Ukraine’s alleged hopelessness. These are similar to the Kremlin’s earlier negotiation tactics which tried to convince the United States and the West generally that Ukrainian defenses were going to collapse such that Ukraine should preemptively capitulate.[6]
The Kremlin is fundamentally interested only in buying time to resolve the war on the battlefield while Russia simultaneously reaps the benefits of economic cooperation with the United States. State Duma Defense Committee First Deputy Chairperson Alexei Zhuravlyov stated on October 21 that Russia must “press” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on the battlefield and force Ukraine to “capitulate.”[7] Zhuravlyov added that Russia should not rely on diplomacy with the United States because Russian “successes on the ground” will strengthen Russia’s negotiating position.[8] Russian Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov similarly claimed that Russian forces maintain the “complete strategic initiative” and are conducting a “relentless offensive” in all key areas of the frontline.[9]
Russian forces are not winning on the battlefield, however, particularly as Ukrainian forces have stymied the planned Russian offensive to seize Donetsk Oblast. ISW has observed evidence that Russian forces suffered a net loss of 241 square kilometers of territory in Ukraine since September 1, 2026. The average rate of daily Russian advances has significantly declined since 2025, with an average of 0.25 square kilometers per day so far in 2026. Ukrainian forces have, comparatively, been contesting and seizing the operational initiative across several sectors of the frontline throughout 2026, including most recently in the Lyman direction with Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi which liberated over 270 square kilometers of territory and thwarted the Russian military command’s plan to encircle the Fortress Belt.[10] Russian forces are also facing mounting monthly casualties while the Russian recruitment rate continues to fall short of its loss rate.[11] Russian forces have suffered almost 37,000 casualties thus far in October 2026 — much higher than the 31,270 casualties for all of October 2025.[12] The Kremlin may face mounting challenges in the coming months, should Ukraine continue to contest the operational initiative and disrupt Russian offensive plans, potentially further pushing Russian commanders to urge Putin to conduct a mobilization in some form.[13]
The Kremlin is likely actively seeking economic cooperation with the United States as Russia faces significant financial strain. Sources familiar with the matter told Bloomberg on October 22 that even a few more months of continued war could exact lasting financial damage on Russian state-owned oil company Rosneft, as Ukrainian strikes against Rosneft’s oil refineries have significantly reduced the company’s profits and increased its debt.[14] Bloomberg added that repeated Ukrainian strikes have prevented Rosneft from completing repairs and restarting refinery operations and that strikes against complex secondary units that often include Western-sourced parts, like catalytic crackers, reformers, and hydrocrackers, are particularly difficult to repair. Russia remains highly susceptible to international sanctions that restrict its access to the technologically advanced components needed to repair the equipment damaged after Ukraine’s strikes.[15] The Kremlin is therefore pushing the United States for various forms of economic relief, so that Russia can continue funding its war against Ukraine.[16] The Kremlin has continuously sought to extract economic concessions during negotiations to alleviate the pressure on its oil industry — including restrictions on Ukrainian strikes against refineries and the relaxation of US sanctions against diesel exports — while expressing little real interest in ending the war.[17]
Russian forces conducted a massive missile and drone strike against Ukraine overnight on October 21 to 22 following the October 21 meeting between Witkoff and Putin — a continuation of Russia’s pattern of launching large strike packages in the days before and after major peace talks. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russian forces conducted a massive combined missile and drone strike primarily targeting Kyiv City and using an unspecified number of Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles and 210 long-range drones, 110 of which were jet-powered.[18] Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Russian forces conducted three waves of ballistic missile strikes against Kyiv City using 21 missiles, damaging residential, energy, railway, and commercial infrastructure.[19] Zelensky stated that Russian strikes targeted 12 Ukrainian oblasts, killing at least two people and injuring at least 34 people. Russian forces regularly conduct massive strikes in the days right before and after bilateral and trilateral talks, such as the August 2025 US-Russia Alaska summit, the November 2025 US-Ukraine talks in Geneva, the November 2025 US-Russia talks in Moscow, the December 2025 US-Ukrainian-European and US-Russian talks, and the January-February 2026 US-Ukrainian-Russian talks in Abu Dhabi.[20]
Russian forces struck Kyiv City with cluster munitions to purposely harm the civilian population, likely as part of wider Russian efforts to distract from Ukraine’s recent battlefield successes and ultimately force Ukraine into capitulation by making daily life untenable.
Zelensky stated that Russian forces struck Pechersk Raion, the historic center of Kyiv City, with three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads that have a dispersion diameter of 400 meters.
[21] The strikes damaged monastery buildings and other civilian infrastructure near the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra and the Holy Presentation Monastery.
Zelensky noted that there were no military targets in the area and that the objective of the strikes was to cause widespread destruction.
[22] Kyiv City Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko stated that Russian forces also struck metro infrastructure on the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River in Kyiv City and damaged six ambulances at an ambulance station in the city.
[23] Ukrainian Presidential Advisor on Defense Technologies Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov stated that each Iskander-M ballistic missile’s cluster warhead releases 45 submunitions that detonate in the air and noted that the objective of the strikes was to destroy a portion of the historic center and injure as many people as possible.
[24] Cluster munitions have a wide area of effect and are designed to kill enemy personnel or destroy light vehicles, underscoring Russia’s intent to maximize civilian harm and suffering.
Cluster munitions historically have a high failure rate, and unexploded bomblets can cause lasting danger for civilians living in affected areas, further demonstrating Russia‘s aim to terrorize civilians.

articles.summary: Azerbaijan expands its economic footprint in Georgia with $3.6 billion in investment  AzerNews
articles.full_text:
Azerbaijan’s economic partnership with Georgia continues to play an important role in the development of the South Caucasus. In 2025, Azerbaijan ranked as Georgia’s second-largest source of foreign direct investment, according to revised data published by Georgia’s National Statistics Office (Geostat) in August 2026. This achievement highlights the importance of Azerbaijani capital in Georgia’s investment landscape and provides a strong foundation for examining the wider economic relationship between the two neighbouring countries.
The latest figures announced in October 2026 further illustrate the scale of this partnership. More than 5,500 companies operating in Georgia have Azerbaijani investment, while the total volume of Azerbaijani investment in the country stands at $3.6 billion, according to Azerbaijan’s Ambassador to Georgia, Faig Guliyev. These figures demonstrate the extensive business connections between the two economies and the role of Azerbaijani investors in Georgia’s commercial environment.
The investment relationship also continued throughout 2026. According to Geostat, Azerbaijani direct investment in Georgia reached $45.3 million during the first half of the year. This figure reflects investment recorded during January–June 2026, while the $3.6 billion figure represents the overall investment volume cited by the Azerbaijani ambassador. Together, these indicators illustrate both ongoing investment activity and the broader scale of Azerbaijani economic engagement in Georgia.
The significance of these investments extends across multiple areas of economic activity. Azerbaijani businesses operating in Georgia can access local customers, develop commercial partnerships and participate in regional supply chains. Their activities can support employment, business services and infrastructure development, while Georgian companies can benefit from closer connections with Azerbaijani investors and the wider regional market.
Trade represents another important dimension of bilateral cooperation. The annual trade turnover between Azerbaijan and Georgia stands at approximately $1.4 billion, with both countries aiming to increase the figure to $2 billion. Achieving this objective would expand commercial opportunities for producers, exporters, transport companies and service providers across both economies.
Energy cooperation provides a longstanding foundation for these economic ties. The Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan oil pipeline and the South Caucasus gas pipeline connect Azerbaijan’s energy resources with international markets through Georgian territory. These routes support energy exports, transit services and regional connectivity, reinforcing the economic importance of cooperation between the two countries.
Transport infrastructure adds another dimension to this partnership. The Middle Corridor links Central Asia and the Caspian Sea with Azerbaijan, Georgia, Türkiye and European markets. The Baku–Tbilisi–Kars railway forms a key component of this network, creating opportunities for freight transportation, logistics services and investment in related infrastructure. As international trade develops, companies in both countries can benefit from expanded cargo flows and stronger commercial connections.
The geographical positions of Azerbaijan and Georgia create complementary advantages. Azerbaijan serves as a gateway across the Caspian Sea, connecting the South Caucasus with Central Asian economies. Georgia provides access towards the Black Sea and Türkiye, linking regional transport routes with wider international markets. Their cooperation therefore supports economic activity extending beyond bilateral trade and investment.
Looking ahead, the partnership offers opportunities in renewable energy, electricity transmission, tourism, agriculture, manufacturing and digital services. Azerbaijani investment can contribute capital and commercial expertise, while Georgia’s transport links and business environment offer opportunities for companies seeking regional expansion. Cooperation in these sectors can broaden the economic relationship and encourage greater participation by private businesses.
The regional significance of this partnership lies in its combination of investment, trade, energy and transport connectivity. Azerbaijan’s second-place position among Georgia’s foreign direct investors in 2025, the continued investment recorded in 2026 and the presence of more than 5,500 Azerbaijani-invested companies illustrate the breadth of their economic relationship.
By expanding these connections, Azerbaijan and Georgia can strengthen their commercial ties, create new opportunities for businesses and reinforce the South Caucasus as a bridge between the Caspian region and international markets. Their shared economic interests provide a substantial platform for continued cooperation and regional prosperity.

articles.summary: Ukraine and Georgia Reaffirm Mutual Support for Territorial Integrity, Discuss Russian Attacks and Energy Assistance  frontnews.eu
articles.full_text:
Ukraine and Georgia have reaffirmed their mutual commitment to supporting each other’s sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity within internationally recognised borders, as senior diplomats met in Tbilisi to discuss Russia’s continued attacks on Ukraine, humanitarian assistance and prospects for closer bilateral cooperation.
Ukraine’s Chargé d’Affaires in Georgia, Dmytro Berezhnyi, met Georgian First Deputy Foreign Minister Giorgi Zurabashvili on Thursday, October 22, for talks covering regional security, bilateral relations and international cooperation.
During the meeting, Berezhnyi briefed the Georgian official on the latest developments in Ukraine, including the consequences of Russian missile and drone strikes targeting civilian facilities and critical infrastructure.
The Ukrainian diplomat highlighted the civilian casualties caused by the attacks and the continuing damage to infrastructure essential to the country’s civilian population.
Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to respecting and supporting Ukraine’s and Georgia’s sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity within their internationally recognised borders.
The diplomats also expressed their readiness to further develop mutually beneficial bilateral relations across areas of shared interest and maintain coordinated efforts within international and regional organisations.
Particular attention was given to cooperation within the Organisation for Democracy and Economic Development – GUAM, a regional grouping comprising Georgia, Ukraine, Azerbaijan and Moldova.
Georgia Highlights Opportunities for Ukraine Through Middle Corridor
Zurabashvili emphasised the potential opportunities for Ukraine arising from Georgia’s strategic infrastructure projects, particularly the development of the Middle Corridor, a transport and trade route connecting Asia and Europe through Central Asia, the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus.
The corridor has gained increasing attention as countries seek to diversify international trade routes and strengthen transport connectivity between Europe and Asia.
Ukraine Seeks Continued Georgian Assistance for Energy Sector
Berezhnyi thanked the Georgian government for its political support for Ukraine within international and regional organisations, as well as for the humanitarian assistance provided since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
He also expressed hope that Georgia would continue providing humanitarian assistance to support Ukraine’s energy sector, which has faced repeated Russian missile and drone attacks.
The discussions highlighted both countries’ stated commitment to maintaining diplomatic engagement, strengthening bilateral cooperation and coordinating their positions in international forums.
The meeting took place against the backdrop of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine and the unresolved territorial conflicts involving the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

articles.summary: Uzbekistan’s U.S. Package: What Supports the $12 Billion Figure?  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan announced a package of 54 agreements and prospective initiatives that it valued at about $12 billion during U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Samarkand on October 19. The Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade lists engine supplies from GE Aerospace for new Uzbekistan Airways aircraft as part of the package. The investment ministry makes that value conditional on implementation. The presidency’s account says a comprehensive implementation program will be developed for the agreements and initiatives.
October’s $12 billion may include projects still awaiting finance or development, but the values assigned to them must have an identifiable basis in project estimates or specific transactions. The official announcements identify counterparties and sectors, but the evidence examined does not provide the individual values needed to reconstruct the $12 billion total.
Earlier Announcements and Additional Value
In November 2025, Donald Trump announced that Uzbekistan would undertake roughly $35 billion in purchases and investment in American sectors over the following three years. The stated total did not separate the amounts assigned to purchases and investment. Uzbekistani purchases from American suppliers and investment in American sectors cannot be counted as an equivalent inflow of U.S. capital into Uzbekistan. Purchasing American equipment and receiving American investment give Uzbekistani participants different roles in the financing and implementation of projects.
In September 2026, Investment Minister Laziz Kudratov said projects worth $7 billion had already been completed within a $35 billion portfolio. UzDaily described the figure as one-fifth of the value of the previous year’s agreements, without identifying the completed projects or defining completion. A transaction-level account would show what equipment was delivered, which facilities were commissioned, and what contract payments were made, giving the value and completion date of each transaction.
October’s $12 billion cannot be added to the earlier figures without reconciling the transactions included in each package and the values assigned to them. The matching $35 billion figures do not establish that Kudratov and Trump referred to the same transaction list. An October agreement could introduce a fresh transaction or add obligations within an existing project, but it could also cover work already reflected in an earlier valuation. A company’s reappearance in successive announcements does not establish which relationship applies.
What the Agreements Establish
American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies announced an October 19 agreement with Uzbekistan Technological Metals Complex and the Fund for Reconstruction and Development, advancing their November 2025 memorandum. ReElement’s release describes a further stage of technical and commercial work under an existing partnership, but it provides no valuation showing how that work contributes to the $12 billion total.
The companies report successful processing of Uzbek-sourced tungsten into high-purity oxide. The planned demonstration at ReElement’s U.S. facilities is intended to evaluate commercial viability, processing efficiency, and scalability; preliminary engineering and economic modeling concern possible refining operations in Uzbekistan.
In the financial sector, the investment ministry describes Franklin Templeton, Oppenheimer, Citigroup, and BlackRock as helping to attract capital, but does not explain whether or how these arrangements contribute to the $12 billion total. On October 21, InfinBANK announced a planned $300 million Eurobond placement arranged by Oppenheimer. This is proposed borrowing by InfinBANK, not a disclosed $300 million investment by Oppenheimer or a valuation of its arranging services.
The Central Bank’s October 21 account of the Samarkand meetings describes cooperation on financial infrastructure and reserve management but announces no financing amounts. Its earlier memorandum with BlackRock, signed in September, concerns cooperation on reserve management and expressly creates no investment mandate, transaction, or financial commitment for either party.
The presidency’s account of the Wabtec discussions covers locomotive supply, servicing, and local production but does not specify a procurement value or financing amount. The October 19 readout discusses participation by U.S. financial institutions, maintenance in Uzbekistan, component manufacturing, and personnel training.
In February 2026, the U.S. Export-Import Bank announced a heads-of-terms agreement advancing the bilateral industrial and infrastructure framework established the previous November. Further discussions in June focused on accelerating joint projects, but neither announcement identifies project-specific loan approvals or committed financing amounts. The October locomotive discussions with Wabtec referenced U.S. financial institutions but did not identify EXIM or disclose financing commitments.
Procurement, Borrowing, and Public Exposure
The conversion of eight options in November 2025 brought Uzbekistan Airways’ firm Boeing order to 22 aircraft. The September 2025 agreement had comprised a firm order for 14 aircraft and options for eight more. The U.S. Commerce Department attached an approximately $8.5 billion valuation to the agreement for up to 22 aircraft. The firm order does not by itself establish how much Uzbekistan Airways has borrowed. The official October accounts do not identify the earlier aircraft order as a component of the $12 billion package.
At a January 2026 press conference, the airline’s chairman put the start of aircraft deliveries around the end of 2030, with the schedule extending over three to four years. He cited expected 2025 net profit of more than $100 million to defend the purchase’s affordability, while declining to disclose the contract price. The chairman has stated the airline’s intention to borrow, but the sources examined do not establish agreed repayment terms or guarantees for the new order. Affordability depends on how the actual price and payment schedule relate to debt service and operating cash flows, rather than on the headline valuation alone.
Government guarantees on earlier aircraft loans show that repayment risk can extend beyond the airline itself. Those guarantees are recorded in the airline’s 2024 consolidated accounts and predate the new Boeing order; they do not establish whether its financing carries comparable guarantees. A guarantee can create contingent public exposure without making the entire purchase price an immediate budget expense. The new order’s public exposure therefore depends on its own borrowing and guarantee terms.
Implementation and Public Accountability
In March, Uzbekistan’s Agriculture Ministry reported that 33 irrigation systems had been installed in cooperation with Valmont across 1,569 hectares. Valmont also appears in the investment ministry’s October announcement. The systems are in Jizzakh and Tashkent regions. The ministry gives no dollar contribution from those installations to Kudratov’s $7 billion completion claim.
The government could show how it reached $12 billion by identifying the agreements and initiatives counted in the total and the values assigned to them. Such a breakdown should state each instrument’s status, identify its counterparties, and give the valuation basis and implementation period for the activity counted. Its account of the financing arrangements would specify who purchases or invests, who borrows, and who provides any public guarantee; procurement and financing for the same asset would be reconciled within the total. The government could publish these distinctions while protecting commercially sensitive clauses.
New locomotives supported by reliable servicing could improve transport performance, and domestic mineral refining could retain more processing activity in Uzbekistan. Their regional contribution would depend on connections with neighboring transport and production systems; their financing would determine repayment obligations and public exposure. The published announcements do not establish how the $12 billion total was calculated. They also provide insufficient detail on project costs, expected revenues, and financing terms for investors to assess affordability or judge whether expected returns justify the costs. The promised implementation program could address these gaps if published with an itemized account of what the total includes, how its components were valued, and their costs, revenue assumptions, and financing arrangements.

Central Asia's two economic drivers, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, seem satisfied with the results of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's visit to the region. But Astana and Tashkent both want to see more done to "translate political agreements into concrete investments."
Rubio led a large American delegation that participated in a business forum in the Uzbek city of Samarkand on October 19. The same day he met with the foreign ministers of all five Central Asian states within the C5+1 format and held one-on-one talks with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.
The Uzbek hosts had the most reason to be satisfied with the outcome of the Samarkand events, announcing investment deals covering a variety of economic sectors potentially worth $12 billion. Uzbek officials said an action plan would be developed to ensure implementation of the agreements, while also announcing Uzbekistan's accession to the Artemis Accords, a US initiative to promote peaceful space exploration.
Mirziyoyev lauded the results while acknowledging that Uzbekistan needed to do more to make the country's investment climate more transparent and predictable. He indicated that a US-Uzbek business council would work to make systematic improvements. "Investors coming to Uzbekistan should be able to start doing business immediately, without wasting time on administrative procedures," Mirziyoyev stated.
While affirming that bilateral relations had "reached a qualitatively new level," he emphasized that there is still lots of room for growth.
"The need for further expansion of economic ties based on a strong political partnership was emphasized," Mirziyoyev said, referring to his discussions with Rubio.
Kazakhstan's leadership also appears content with Rubio's visit, even though no specific US-Kazakh business deals were announced. The headline of a commentary published by the Kazinform state news agency stated; "Rubio's Samarkand visit gives fresh momentum to US-Central Asia ties."
Astana was perhaps most pleased to hear that the United States will not be pursuing a zero-sum economic policy in the region that would force Central Asian states to chose between the American and Chinese models of development in key areas, especially digital technologies and artificial intelligence.
Kazakhstan is a member of both Pax Silica, a US-led initiative governing IT/AI development, and a similar Chinese-orchestrated grouping called WAICO. The Kazinform commentary stressed that Rubio in Samarkand "was not asking regional countries to abandon their existing partnerships with Russia, China or other powers," adding that "this approach is consistent with the multi-vector foreign policy pursued by Kazakhstan."
Like Uzbekistan, however, Kazakhstan wants the United States to do more. An immediate step that Washington can take is the repeal of Jackson-Vanik trade restrictions, Kazakh officials believe. The Trump administration supports the repeal of Jackson-Vanik, but Rubio in Samarkand told journalists that the Republican-controlled Congress "just hasn't gotten around to it, but we hope that they will."
The Kazinform commentary indicated that Astana will be paying close attention to how Washington follows up on its vision for enhanced trade ties, as outlined in a joint statement issued after the Samarkand meetings. "Implementation of commercial agreements will be another important measure of progress," the commentary noted. "The figures announced in Washington and Samarkand represent contracts and planned transactions rather than investments already completed, while the C5+1 statement establishes shared objectives without binding financial commitments."
According to Kazakh media, Rubio indicated that he may pay a visit to Kazakhstan at some point after the upcoming G20 gathering in Florida in mid-December. Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Mirziyoyev are scheduled to participate in those discussions.
Turkmenistan also expressed interest in expanding bilateral ties with the United States, as well as its Central Asian neighbors. A Turkmen Foreign Ministry statement reiterated Ashgabat's intent to integrate into the emerging regional trade system, especially trans-Caspian initiatives. It also endorsed efforts to create "favorable conditions for stimulating corporate activity and attracting investment," and called for an increase in educational exchanges with the United States.
While the Samarkand meetings appeared to firm up the US trade position in Central Asia, China offered a reminder that it is determined to remain the dominant economic player in the region for the foreseeable future. On October 19, the same day Tajikistan's foreign minister was participating in the Samarkand discussions, Tajik leader Emomali Rahmon was hosting China's premier, Li Qiang, in Dushanbe. Pointing out that bilateral trade volume amounts to about $2.5 billion during the first eight months of 2026, Li said Beijing was ready to help Tajikistan implement "priority projects," including the country's AI capabilities.

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has appointed Giorgi Zurabashvili as his special representative for relations with Russia, a post that has been vacant since December 2025.
Georgia and Russia have had no diplomatic relations since the 2008 war, which ended with Russia recognising the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, two breakaway regions internationally recognised as part of Georgia. Despite the absence of diplomatic ties, Russia and Georgia maintain trade and economic relations, while the Geneva International Discussions and the special representative’s position provide channels for dialogue.
Kobakhidze announced the appointment on Wednesday, describing the role as important for maintaining dialogue with Moscow amid the absence of diplomatic relations between Georgia and Russia.
‘The peaceful resolution of the conflict with the Russian Federation, the preservation and development of existing trade and economic relations, and maintaining ongoing dialogue on humanitarian issues are among our country’s most important priorities’, Kobakhidze said.
He added that, alongside the Geneva International Discussions, the prime minister’s special representative played a key role in pursuing these objectives.
Kobakhidze described Zurabashvili as an experienced diplomat who had held several senior public service positions over the years, including directorships at various departments of the Foreign Ministry and an ambassadorship.
Zurabashvili was appointed Deputy Foreign Minister in 2024 and First Deputy Foreign Minister on 1 July 2025.
‘We are confident that Giorgi Zurabashvili will use his knowledge and experience to fulfil the responsibilities entrusted to him as the Prime Minister’s special representative’, Kobakhidze added.
In response to a journalist’s question, Kobakhidze stated that the appointment did not signal a new stage in Georgia’s relations with Russia.
Zurabashvili will retain his position at the Foreign Ministry. However, Kobakhidze said that he would represent Georgia in relations with Russia in his capacity as the Prime Minister’s special representative.
‘I will do everything in my power to fulfil the tasks that Georgia needs me to carry out’, Zurabashvili said.
The position of the Prime Minister’s special representative for relations with Russia became vacant in December 2025, when Giorgi Kajaja left the post.
Before Kajaja, Zurab Abashidze held the position for 12 years, from 2012 to 2024, serving as the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia, in the so-called Abashidze–Karasin format, a bilateral dialogue mechanism between Georgia and Russia.
On 6 October, the Foreign Ministry announced that Abashidze had been appointed Georgia’s non-resident ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Albania.
For ease of reading, we choose not to use qualifiers such as ‘de facto’, ‘unrecognised’, or ‘partially recognised’ when discussing institutions or political positions within Abkhazia, Nagorno-Karabakh, and South Ossetia. This does not imply a position on their status.

articles.title: The Region in Brief - The Armenian Weekly
articles.summary: The Region in Brief  The Armenian Weekly
articles.full_text:
Artsakh
Displaced Armenians from Artsakh held a demonstration in Yerevan this week, delivering letters to foreign embassies calling for the right of return and the protection of Armenian cultural heritage to be included in international diplomatic discussions and the upcoming COP17 biodiversity conference. Alvard Zakaryan, a member of Artsakh’s Public Council, emphasized that about 150,000 displaced Armenians remain committed to returning to their homeland, calling for international guarantees for a safe, dignified and sustainable return.
The demonstration coincided with renewed warnings over Azerbaijan’s efforts to reclassify Armenian cultural monuments in occupied Artsakh as Caucasian Albanian heritage.
Armenian heritage watchdog Monument Watch challenged claims presented to about 150 foreign diplomats and international representatives during a September visit to the historic monasteries of Dadivank and Gandzasar, accompanied by Azerbaijani presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev. Azerbaijani representatives alleged that medieval Armenian khachkars at Dadivank had been manufactured during Artsakh’s independence and artificially aged with vinegar. Monument Watch rejected the claims, citing inscriptions dating from 1172 to 1190, some documented as early as 1911, decades before Artsakh’s independence. The organization described the presentation as part of a systematic effort to deny the Armenian origins of the region’s religious and cultural heritage.
Meanwhile, Artsakh’s Cultural Heritage Ombudsman’s Office announced a series of publications ahead of COP17 documenting alleged environmental destruction under Azerbaijani control. The initiative raises concerns over deforestation, large-scale construction, biodiversity loss and damage to historic cemeteries and archaeological sites, warning that some consequences may be irreversible. The office is calling for independent investigations, international oversight and accountability for potential acts of genocide.
Azerbaijan
Azerbaijan has declared 31 Turkish citizens personae non gratae, barring them from entering the country amid an unusual diplomatic dispute between two states that have long characterized their relationship as “one nation, two states.”
The decision, announced by Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry on Oct. 21, targets prominent Turkish political figures, journalists, religious commentators and social media personalities, including New Welfare Party leader Fatih Erbakan, Turkish lawmaker Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu and representatives of the Islamist Free Cause Party (HÜDA PAR).
Baku accused those listed of publishing statements targeting Azerbaijan’s sovereignty, national security, constitutional order and political leadership. It further alleged that some had encouraged the violent overthrow of the government or incited religious hatred and extremism.
The dispute follows growing controversy over restrictions on the wearing of Islamic headscarves in Azerbaijani schools. New school uniform regulations introduced in September have reportedly resulted in girls wearing hijabs being turned away from educational institutions, prompting criticism from conservative and religious figures in Turkey. Azerbaijani authorities have characterized some of that criticism as interference in the country’s internal affairs.
By Oct. 19, Azerbaijan’s Prosecutor General’s Office had already placed seven individuals residing in Turkey on an international wanted list, accusing them of promoting religious extremism and calling for the forcible seizure of power.
Georgia
Georgia’s Constitutional Court began hearings in Batumi on Wednesday, Oct. 21, in a case brought by the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to outlaw five major opposition groups, raising serious concerns about the future of political pluralism in the country.
The lawsuit, signed by 88 lawmakers, targets the United National Movement, Coalition for Change, Strong Georgia–Lelo, the Federalist Party and former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia’s For Georgia party. Georgian Dream lawmakers allege that the organizations have violated Article 23 of the Georgian Constitution through activities and political objectives aimed at forcibly changing the country’s constitutional order.
The opposition parties reject the allegations, describing the proceedings as an attempt to eliminate political competition and consolidate the ruling party’s control. According to Civil Georgia, representatives of four of the five targeted parties participated in the hearings, while the Federalists refused to legitimize the proceedings through courtroom participation. Independent journalists were also prohibited from filming inside the courtroom, with recording rights reserved for the Georgian Public Broadcaster.
The hearings are scheduled to continue through Oct. 23, with a final ruling expected by June 2027. The case comes amid longstanding political tensions following Georgia’s disputed 2024 parliamentary elections and mounting international criticism of the government’s democratic record.
Russia
Armenia’s increasingly uncertain relationship with Russian-led institutions came under renewed scrutiny this week after representatives of the four other Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) member states issued a report warning of potentially severe economic consequences if Yerevan’s membership is suspended.
Prepared by representatives of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, the report examines the implications of Armenia’s continued pursuit of closer integration with the European Union, warning that the country’s European ambitions could create legal incompatibilities with its existing EAEU obligations. The four member states maintain that they have grounds to consider suspending the application of the EAEU Treaty to Armenia, potentially even before Yerevan holds a referendum on its future integration priorities.
The report projects that suspending Armenia’s participation could result in a 15.6% contraction in GDP, a 14.9-percentage-point rise in inflation, and a 55.6% reduction in trade with EAEU members. It also estimates that the price of Russian natural gas supplied to Armenia could increase by 69%, from $177.50 to $300 per 1,000 cubic meters, raising annual import costs from about $389 million to $657 million.
Other projected consequences include a sharp reduction in remittances from Russia, more restrictive employment conditions for Armenian citizens working in EAEU countries, higher railway freight costs and tighter customs and sanitary controls. The report also warns of significant declines in Armenian exports and reexports, potentially disrupting businesses reliant on access to the Eurasian market.
Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Kremlin had not yet reviewed the report, while its authors said the other EAEU members were not seeking Armenia’s departure from the bloc.
Political analyst Vahe Davtyan described the report as a particularly strong political signal, noting that the economic consequences of Armenia’s suspension would be considerably more severe for Yerevan than for the remaining member states.
ARF member and secretary of the opposition Armenia Alliance Artur Khachatryan likewise warned that even if only half of the projected economic losses materialized, the consequences for Armenia could be extremely serious. He argued that the government must confront the practical implications of any departure from the EAEU, including the availability and cost of alternative energy supplies.
Meanwhile, Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) Secretary-General Taalatbek Masadykov suggested that Armenia could still reconsider its decision to freeze participation in the Russian-led security alliance. “Time passes, people reconsider their positions, and the situation in the world changes,” Masadykov said, expressing hope that Armenian authorities and the public would reach a decision on whether to remain in the organization.
Although Armenia has suspended active participation in CSTO activities and stopped paying membership contributions, it remains a member under the organization’s legal framework. Masadykov noted that decisions concerning membership ultimately rest with the leaders of CSTO member states. Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan, however, rejected the prospect of returning, telling reporters that he could not envision Armenia resuming its participation in the alliance.
Separately, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova rejected renewed media allegations questioning the safety of Armenia’s Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant. Responding to reports circulated by Azerbaijani outlets, Zakharova said the allegations lacked a factual basis and defended the safety record of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom, the plant’s principal technical partner.
She suggested that the timing of the reports, amid COP17-related attention on Armenia, could indicate political motivations, including efforts to undermine Armenian-Russian cooperation in nuclear energy.

articles.title: U.S. Promotes Small Nuclear Reactors in Uzbekistan - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: U.S. Promotes Small Nuclear Reactors in Uzbekistan  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
The United States is promoting small modular nuclear reactors in Uzbekistan as Tashkent develops its nuclear power sector with Russia. Secretary of State Marco Rubio promoted the technology during his October 19 visit to Samarkand, linking it to rising energy demand.
“We’re introducing U.S. small modular reactors and modernizing the Uzbek electric grid and gas distribution network,” Rubio told the U.S.-Uzbekistan Business and Investment Council. He said the cooperation would help the government keep pace with growing energy demand.
Rubio did not name a reactor supplier or announce financing or a construction schedule for an American plant.
Uzbekistan’s interest predates Rubio’s visit. In November 2025, the country expressed interest in studying designs from Holtec, GE Hitachi, and NuScale, according to the World Nuclear Association. Tashkent has pursued those discussions alongside its current nuclear partnership with Russia.
Small modular reactors generally have an electrical capacity of up to 300 megawatts per unit, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency. Factories can manufacture their components and assemble them on site. Utilities can add smaller units in stages as demand increases.
For Uzbekistan, nuclear power forms part of an effort to expand electricity supply as domestic gas production declines. Once a net gas exporter, the country became a net importer in 2023. Gas output fell 16.3% year-on-year in January-August 2026, increasing pressure on supplies. The World Nuclear Association puts natural gas at 76% of Uzbekistan’s electricity output in 2023. Reducing the amount burned in power stations could ease import needs and leave more available for industry, including petrochemicals.
Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom is developing Uzbekistan’s first nuclear complex in the Forish district of the Jizzakh region. The design combines two large Russian VVER-1000 reactors with two smaller RITM-200N units, providing about 2.1 gigawatts of capacity. The smaller reactors are each rated at 55 megawatts.
Presidents Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Vladimir Putin launched the project by video link in June, accompanied by a concrete pouring ceremony. The development has expanded substantially since the countries agreed in 2024 to build a plant consisting of six small reactors.
The published schedule envisages a technical launch of the first small unit in late 2029, with the larger units following in the 2030s. Nuclear generation is therefore several years away. Uzbekistan must also improve the networks that deliver electricity to homes and businesses.
Following a nationwide referendum on the issue, Kazakhstan is also investing in nuclear power. Its planned Balkhash plant, near Ulken on Lake Balkhash, will use Russian technology. A nuclear agreement signed in May envisages two VVER-1200 reactors with a combined capacity of about 2.4 gigawatts. Kazakhstan’s Atomic Energy Agency put the project’s cost at approximately $16.5 billion, including security and supporting infrastructure.
Kazakhstan’s strategy calls for at least three nuclear power plants by 2050. China National Nuclear Corporation has been selected to lead the second project. The country is the world’s largest uranium producer, but developing power stations also requires foreign reactor technology and expertise.
Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have begun cooperating on nuclear safety. Officials met in Tashkent in August to discuss environmental monitoring and potential cross-border effects, with Uzbekistan also proposing a regional center to train nuclear specialists.
The nuclear discussions form part of Washington’s push for closer commercial ties with Central Asia. Rubio’s Samarkand visit included talks with Mirziyoyev and a C5+1 ministerial meeting with all five Central Asian countries. The gathering followed the November 2025 White House summit with the region’s presidents.
Speaking to reporters in Samarkand, Rubio acknowledged Washington’s limited engagement with the region in the past.
“Central Asia has just not gotten the level of attention from our policymakers over the last 20 years that it deserves, but that’s changing,” he said.
The C5+1 format grew from a proposal advanced by Kazakhstan, formally launching in 2015, when then-Secretary of State John Kerry attended its inaugural ministerial meeting in Samarkand. Recent discussions have placed greater emphasis on critical minerals and investment in regional infrastructure. At this month’s meeting, the governments backed more mineral processing within Central Asia and further development of the Trans-Caspian Trade Route, also known as the Middle Corridor.
Uzbekistan announced 54 agreements and prospective initiatives worth about $12 billion during Rubio’s visit. The package spans several industries, with energy infrastructure and critical minerals among its priorities. The announcement did not specify how much of the total had secured financing.
The two countries also launched an Enhanced Strategic Partnership Dialogue, while Uzbekistan signed the U.S.-led Artemis Accords on peaceful space exploration. At the business council, Mirziyoyev proposed a joint program for trade and technological cooperation through 2035.
For Uzbekistan, considering American reactors broadens its options as electricity demand grows and domestic gas production declines. Rosatom’s existing project remains central to its nuclear plans, while talks with U.S. suppliers could widen its choice of reactor designs and partners.

articles.title: Georgia appoints new special envoy for relations with Russia: what does it mean? - JAMnews
articles.summary: Georgia appoints new special envoy for relations with Russia: what does it mean?  JAMnews
articles.full_text:
On 21 October, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze appointed Giorgi Zurabashvili, the first deputy foreign minister, as his special representative for relations with Russia. The post had remained vacant since December 2025.
The announcement came on the same day that the Constitutional Court began hearing on the merits a lawsuit by the ruling party seeking to ban five opposition parties.
Opposition figures have interpreted the timing as a signal to Moscow. Kobakhidze, for his part, insists that the appointment does not mark a new phase in relations with Russia.
What Kobakhidze said
The prime minister announced the appointment at a briefing in the government administration. Asked by a journalist whether this marked the beginning of a new phase in efforts to reset relations with Russia, he said it did not.
Kobakhidze said the Georgian Interests Section at the Swiss embassy in Moscow had been working actively. However, the government had decided that it needed an additional channel alongside the section to “resolve the conflict peacefully, maintain humanitarian ties and develop trade and economic relations”.
The prime minister also denied that the decision was linked to recent restrictions Russia had imposed on products from Georgian companies.
“Of course, work on these issues is a priority overall, but this was certainly not the basis for the decision,” Kobakhidze said.
Asked about restoring diplomatic relations between Georgia and Russia, Kobakhidze said an obstacle remained: “This situation has not changed, and neither has our position.”
Regarding Russia’s demand that Tbilisi provide Sukhumi and Tskhinvali (the capitals of Abkhazia and South Ossetia) with guarantees of non-use of force, the prime minister said Georgia could not sign an agreement with them because it could not recognise them as independent states in any form.
Giorgi Zurabashvili will also retain his post as first deputy foreign minister, which he has held since July 2025. He previously served as Georgia’s ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to Ireland from 2019 to 2024.
The special envoy role
Since 2012, diplomat Zurab Abashidze had served as Georgia’s special representative for relations with Russia. He held regular meetings with Grigory Karasin, a Russian deputy foreign minister. This channel of talks became known as the “Abashidze–Karasin format”.
In March 2024, Irakli Kobakhidze moved Abashidze to the post of his adviser and appointed Giorgi Kajaya as his replacement. However, the government administration told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that Kajaya left the post on 1 December 2025.
The public learned that the position had remained vacant only in August 2026, when Kobakhidze answered a question from journalists.
Meanwhile, on 6 October 2026, Zurab Abashidze became Georgia’s non-resident ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia and Albania.
“A cynical signal”: opposition reaction
Grigol Gegelia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia–Lelo opposition coalition, whose party the government is seeking to ban, believes that:
“This is a direct, cynical signal that the parties are being banned at Russia’s behest, and that on the very same day, in a synchronised move, a person is appointed to pursue warmer relations with Russia.”
According to Lasha Parulava, a member of the governing council of another opposition party, the United National Movement, the appointment serves no economic purpose and is a symbolic gesture.
“Here, at the Constitutional Court, they are dismantling the pro-Western opposition while, at the same time, appointing a special representative to Russia.”
The founder of the United National Movement and Georgia’s third president, Mikheil Saakashvili, wrote on social media that “the rapid restoration of diplomatic relations with Russia is being prepared without de-occupation, which amounts to formally endorsing capitulation”.
Moscow welcomed the appointment. Konstantin Zatulin, first deputy chairman of the Russian State Duma’s Committee on CIS Affairs, called the decision a step in the right direction.
“The decision to appoint a special representative is a step in the right direction. Relations between Russia and Georgia must develop,” Zatulin said.
Relations with Russia under Georgian Dream
Restoring relations with Russia was one of the main campaign promises of the current ruling party, Georgian Dream. The special representative post was established shortly after it came to power, on 1 November 2012. Following the August 2008 war, Tbilisi and Moscow had communicated directly only through the Geneva International Discussions.
The Abashidze–Karasin format helped restore exports of Georgian wine, mineral water, fruit and vegetables to the Russian market in 2013. The authorities also softened their rhetoric towards Russia.
On 20 June 2019, mass protests broke out in Tbilisi after Russian MP Sergei Gavrilov addressed the Georgian parliament. Russia subsequently suspended direct flights to Georgia. In May 2023, Russian President Vladimir Putin lifted visa requirements for Georgian citizens and restored direct flights.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgian Dream declined to join international sanctions against Russia, saying it wanted to protect Georgia’s economy.
From January to August 2026, Russia accounted for around 62.5% of the value of Georgia’s wine exports.
On 9 October, Russia’s food safety watchdog suspended imports of products from seven Georgian companies. On the same day, Russia’s Foreign Ministry again demanded that Tbilisi provide Sukhumi and Tskhinvali with guarantees of non-use of force and begin delimiting the so-called state borders.

Circular Economy and Rational Resource Use
