articles.title: Ten years of BRI: Infrastructure ambitions to economic transformation - The Financial Express
articles.summary: Ten years of BRI: Infrastructure ambitions to economic transformation  The Financial Express
articles.full_text:
Ten years after joining China’s Belt and Road Initiative, Bangladesh stands at a defining moment. Chinese financing has helped reshape its transport networks, energy infrastructure and investment landscape. The next phase of cooperation must therefore move beyond building infrastructure and toward strengthening industrial capacity, expanding exports and securing sustainable economic growth.
A decade ago, Bangladesh embarked on one of its most consequential development partnerships, opening a new chapter in its economic relationship with China. When Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Dhaka on October 14, 2016, Bangladesh formally joined the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), positioning itself among South Asia’s earliest participants in China’s ambitious connectivity framework. The visit elevated bilateral relations to a strategic partnership of cooperation and generated approximately $40 billion in proposed financing and investment commitments.
Ten years later, the most important question is not simply how much China has invested, but how effectively that cooperation has strengthened Bangladesh’s economic foundations.
The BRI’s first decade has delivered substantial progress in physical connectivity and energy infrastructure, while exposing critical gaps between financial pledges and implementation, rising trade imbalances, and the need for greater investment efficiency. These achievements and limitations deserve equal consideration as Bangladesh plans its next decade of cooperation, shaping the priorities ahead.
The economic ambition underpinning Bangladesh’s BRI participation was considerable. The 2016 commitments included approximately $26 billion for infrastructure and development projects and another $14 billion for joint ventures. Transport, electricity, telecommunications and industrial connectivity dominated the proposed investment portfolio.
However, financial commitments should not be confused with actual disbursements. According to an assessment published by a news outlet, outgoing Chinese Ambassador Yao Wen reported that $4.45 billion had been disbursed for 35 BRI projects by 2023. The assessment noted that comprehensive and updated BRI-specific disbursement figures remained unavailable, limiting independent evaluation of implementation progress.
The central challenge not merely mobilising additional financing, but ensuring timely implementation, transparent procurement and manageable repayment obligations. These policy choices will determine whether cooperation strengthens Bangladesh’s economic foundations. This challenge also sets the stage for the shift from funding to trade and investment.
Trade and investment have become central pillars of Bangladesh–China cooperation. China has remained Bangladesh’s largest trading partner for 16 consecutive years, from 2010 through 2025. According to figures published by the Chinese Embassy in September 2026, bilateral trade reached $12.8 billion in the first half of 2026, up 10.6 percent year on year.
Chinese machinery, industrial equipment, raw materials and intermediate goods support Bangladesh’s manufacturing industries, particularly ready-made garments, leather and electronics. However, the persistent imbalance between imports and exports highlights the need to strengthen Bangladesh’s export capacity. Rather than restricting productive imports, Bangladesh should work with Chinese investors and buyers to expand exports of agricultural products, processed food, seafood, leather goods, pharmaceuticals, home textiles, light engineering products and digital services.
Realising this potential requires more than market access. Bangladesh must improve logistics, product quality, international certification, technology transfer and industrial linkages to diversify beyond its heavy reliance on ready-made garments. China’s zero-tariff market access for eligible Bangladeshi products and the prospect of a bilateral free-trade agreement offer opportunities to advance this agenda.
The priority for the next decade should therefore be to transform the trading relationship into a more balanced and mutually beneficial partnership — one that strengthens domestic industries, creates employment and expands competitive, higher-value exports while gradually narrowing the bilateral trade gap.
Investment trends are particularly noteworthy. China’s foreign direct investment stock reportedly increased from $241 million in 2016 to nearly $2 billion by the end of 2025, representing approximately 700 per cent growth. China became Bangladesh’s third-largest source of FDI stock and its second-largest source of annual net FDI inflows in 2025, contributing $321.15 million.
China has also emerged as Bangladesh’s largest private-sector external creditor. Its share of private-sector long-term external debt reached 34.2 percent in 2025, equivalent to $3.37 billion, compared with $422 million in 2020. This reflects growing financial integration, but also strengthens the case for prudent debt management.
A promising development is the China Economic and Industrial Zone in Anwara, Chattogram, formally launched in July 2026. The zone aims to attract manufacturing investment in textiles, machinery, electronics, and green industries. Such initiatives could transform Chinese engagement from predominantly infrastructure construction into long-term industrial production, employment generation and technology transfer.
Infrastructure remains the most tangible outcome of BRI cooperation. Chinese companies have participated in landmark projects including the Padma Bridge Rail Link, Karnaphuli Tunnel, Chattogram-Cox’s Bazar railway, Chattogram Elevated Expressway, and Dasherkandi Sewage Treatment Plant.
The Padma Bridge Rail Link has strengthened railway connectivity between Dhaka and southwestern Bangladesh, opening opportunities for trade, transportation and regional development. The Karnaphuli Tunnel, inaugurated in 2023, represents another engineering milestone, creating an underwater road connection intended to support Chattogram’s industrial and logistics expansion.
The Padma Multipurpose Bridge, constructed by a Chinese contractor but financed by Bangladesh itself, also demonstrates the wider role of Chinese engineering expertise.
Energy cooperation has similarly contributed to expanding electricity-generation capacity. The 1,320-megawatt Payra Thermal Power Plant, developed through a Bangladesh-China joint venture, stands among the most significant examples. Chinese financing and technical expertise have also supported electricity transmission and other energy projects. However, growing generation capacity must be accompanied by reliable fuel supplies, efficient transmission networks and greater investment in renewable energy.
The achievements of the past decade are significant, but infrastructure alone cannot guarantee sustainable development. The next phase of Bangladesh–China Belt and Road cooperation must focus on converting connectivity into productivity, investment into industrial capacity, and economic partnerships into tangible benefits for businesses and citizens.
Bangladesh should prioritise commercially viable investments, transparent procurement, prudent debt management and stronger domestic industrial participation. Infrastructure projects must be linked to export-oriented manufacturing, renewable energy, technology transfer and skills development to generate quality employment, strengthen local supply chains and increase domestic value addition.
Equally important is establishing clear mechanisms for accountability. A public dashboard tracking project financing, implementation progress and economic outcomes, complemented by independent assessments of value for money, would help ensure that investments deliver measurable benefits.
Bangladesh must also maintain diversified international partnerships, ensuring that cooperation with China complements its relationships with India, Japan, the European Union and multilateral development institutions. Such an approach would preserve policy flexibility while enabling Bangladesh to pursue mutually beneficial investment and trade opportunities.
The central objective for 2027–2036 should be to build stronger domestic industries, diversify exports, develop a skilled workforce and improve Bangladesh’s position in regional and global value chains. Ultimately, the success of the next decade will depend not on how much infrastructure is built, but on how effectively it supports competitive businesses, sustainable growth and inclusive economic prosperity.
The first decade strengthened connectivity; the next must deliver competitiveness. Bangladesh’s greatest achievement will be measured by what it can produce, export and sustain—not simply by what it builds.
Mohammad Saiyedul Islam, PhD, is a Senior Lecturer and Researcher in the School of Overseas Education at Sanming University in China’s Fujian Province.

articles.title: Moscow claims there is no political motive behind restrictions on importing Georgian drinks - OC Media
articles.summary: Moscow claims there is no political motive behind restrictions on importing Georgian drinks  OC Media
articles.full_text:
Russia has denied that the recent introduction of restrictions on some Georgian beverages were politically motivated; Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova described them as routine quality-control measures.
Russia previously banned Georgian wine in 2006, citing health concerns, and later imposed restrictions on Georgian mineral water, including Borjomi and Nabeghlavi. Georgian officials at the time described the measures as politically motivated. In 2019, Moscow again threatened economic measures against Georgia, amid anti-Russian protests in Tbilisi.
At a briefing on Wednesday, Zakharova responded to a question from Nikoloz Mzhavanadze, a UK-sanctioned figure who asked the question on behalf of Tao News, about the restrictions on Georgian drinks.
‘This is not a matter for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It is a matter for Rospotrebnadzor’, Zakharova said, referring to Russia’s consumer protection watchdog.
She said the agency was responsible for checking whether products met Russia’s safety requirements and preventing the import of products from manufacturers it considered dishonest.
‘The restrictions introduced are targeted. We see how an absolutely routine procedure is being turned into some kind of political factor, with people speculating on this topic. There is no political subtext’, Zakharova said.
She added that Russia continued to import products from dozens of Georgian companies and that violations had been identified at only several enterprises. The others, she said, continued to operate in the Russian market, which she described as a priority for Georgia.
On 10 October, it emerged that Russia had temporarily suspended the import and sale of some alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks from several Georgian producers.
The affected products include wine from Teliani Valley, Tbilvino, and Wine Man; wine and brandy from Askaneli Brothers; beer from the Georgian Beer Company; Coca-Cola produced in Georgia; and Nabeglavi mineral water, produced by Healthy Water.
Russia has also introduced wide-reaching import restrictions on Armenian goods in recent years. In a similar vein to the Georgia case, Moscow has claimed they are for quality and safety reasons, while others allege they are politically motivated amid faltering Russia-Armenia relations.
Kobakhidze responds to Russia’s demands
On Wednesday, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze appointed Giorgi Zurabashvili as his special representative for relations with Russia. The post had been vacant since December 2025.
The Diplomatic Society of Georgia said the appointment could signal a move towards restoring diplomatic ties. It also warned that expanding Zurabashvili’s mandate to include conflict resolution risked undermining the Geneva International Discussions and Georgia’s efforts to keep the conflict on the international agenda.
At the same briefing, Kobakhidze responded to a statement from the Russian Foreign Ministry that Moscow continued to require Georgia to provide guarantees of the non-use of force.
Kobakhidze said Georgia could not sign an agreement with Abkhazia or South Ossetia because doing so would imply recognition of the two entities as states.
‘It is impossible, because we cannot recognise the so-called states in any way or form — the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of South Ossetia cannot be recognised by us, even indirectly. Consequently, no agreement can be signed with them. Naturally, this will be the position expressed by the special representative’, Kobakhidze said.
The non-use of force is one of the key issues discussed at the Geneva International Discussions.
Georgia made a unilateral pledge not to use force in 2010 and has repeatedly made unilateral commitments to non-aggression, including at the UN and the EU Parliament, and before all 27 EU member states when signing its Association Agreement with the EU.
For ease of reading, we choose not to use qualifiers such as ‘de facto’, ‘unrecognised’, or ‘partially recognised’ when discussing institutions or political positions within Abkhazia and South Ossetia. This does not imply a position on their status.

articles.title: Sadyr Japarov outlines Kyrgyzstan’s TURKPA priorities - new opportunities for cooperation with Azerbaijan - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: Sadyr Japarov outlines Kyrgyzstan’s TURKPA priorities - new opportunities for cooperation with Azerbaijan  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 22. Kyrgyzstan held the 15th Plenary Session of the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TURKPA) on October 20, with the chairmanship of the organization passing from Kazakhstan to Kyrgyzstan. The new chairmanship under the leadership of Marlen Mamataliev, Speaker of the Jogorku Kenesh (Parliament) of Kyrgyzstan, creates additional opportunities to advance regional initiatives in trade, transport, energy and digitalization, as well as strengthen economic ties between Central Asia and the South Caucasus.
As part of the session, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov received the speakers of the parliaments of TURKPA member states. The president described the meeting as evidence of friendship and mutual trust between brotherly countries and reaffirmed Bishkek’s interest in further developing cooperation. He said the Assembly’s activities are intended to strengthen ties between the countries and deepen cooperation in trade and economic affairs, transport, energy, digitalization and humanitarian matters.
This agenda is becoming particularly important amid the growing role of regional transport routes, expanding trade ties and the need to harmonize rules governing cross-border economic cooperation. Under these circumstances, TURKPA could serve not only as a platform for political dialogue but also as an additional mechanism for advancing legislative measures needed to implement intergovernmental agreements.
One of the main outcomes of the session was the adoption of the Bishkek Declaration and four model laws. Kyrgyzstan also outlined its chairmanship priorities, including digital transformation, legislation governing artificial intelligence, transport and economic connectivity, youth policy, and expanded cultural and humanitarian exchanges. The practical significance of these priorities will depend on how consistently member states incorporate the adopted decisions into their national legislation and use them to develop joint initiatives.
Particular attention should be paid to Mamataliev’s proposal to establish a unified electronic register of TURKPA model laws and prepare an annual analytical report on their implementation. Such a mechanism could provide more systematic monitoring of the application of harmonized legislative approaches, help identify differences in national regulations and determine areas for further legal alignment. For businesses, this could potentially mean more predictable operating conditions in TURKPA member states, although tangible changes would require relevant decisions by national authorities.
One of the most promising areas of Kyrgyzstan’s chairmanship could be the development of transport and economic links between Central Asia and the South Caucasus. Azerbaijan plays an important role in this context, as its geographical position connects Central Asia with the South Caucasus, Türkiye, and European markets. Deeper cooperation between Baku and Bishkek could expand trade and logistics opportunities and enable companies from both countries to participate more actively in regional supply chains.
In October 2026, at a meeting of Central Asian leaders and Azerbaijan in Awaza, Sadyr Japarov proposed considering unified freight transportation tariffs and the creation of a common electronic trading platform.
Parliamentary diplomacy could complement the work of governments and relevant agencies in this area. Legislators could exchange experience in regulating cross-border transportation, discuss ways to simplify procedures for businesses and propose legal mechanisms to support regional projects. However, introducing unified tariffs, establishing a common electronic platform and implementing infrastructure initiatives would require separate intergovernmental agreements, technical preparation and financing.
The development of allied relations between Kyrgyzstan and Azerbaijan creates further opportunities for such cooperation. On October 20, Sadyr Japarov received Speaker of the Parliament of Azerbaijan, Sahiba Gafarova. The sides discussed prospects for cooperation in trade and economic affairs, investment, energy, and transport.
Sadyr Japarov emphasized the special nature of the allied relationship and the importance of consistently implementing existing agreements, including the Treaty on Allied Relations signed in July 2026. Gafarova, in turn, noted the dynamic development of bilateral ties, including interparliamentary cooperation, and stressed the importance of further strengthening relations.
This political foundation creates conditions for advancing bilateral initiatives within a broader multilateral framework. Azerbaijan can use parliamentary contacts to expand engagement with Central Asian countries, while Kyrgyzstan can strengthen its links with the South Caucasus and improve access to regional transport routes. A key outcome of this approach could be closer coordination of legislative and economic initiatives aimed at developing trade and attracting investment.
Digitalization will be another important area of Kyrgyzstan’s chairmanship. During the plenary session, representatives of Kyrgyzstan, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Türkiye and Uzbekistan shared their experience in applying digital technologies in parliamentary work and discussed the legal aspects of artificial intelligence development. Kyrgyzstan presented its transition away from paper-based document management in parliament and the introduction of digital tools, including a system for analyzing legislation. Azerbaijan, in turn, presented its experience with electronic document management, automated stenography and digital engagement with citizens.
Exchanging such practices could provide a basis for joint educational initiatives, recommendations on AI regulation and improvements to electronic parliamentary procedures. The proposed unified register of model laws could also make legislative experience more accessible across member states and increase the transparency of the Assembly’s work.
Alongside economic and technological issues, Kyrgyzstan intends to develop the humanitarian dimension of cooperation. Discussions at the TURKPA session covered the preservation of shared historical and cultural values, expanded youth exchanges and the creation of a common information space. The proposed recommendations envisage cooperation among news agencies, television and radio broadcasters, the development of media literacy and the exchange of experience in using artificial intelligence. These initiatives could strengthen information and public ties between member states, complementing official diplomatic contacts.
The practical results of Kyrgyzstan’s chairmanship will depend on whether the adopted documents and announced priorities are followed up by the Assembly’s commissions, national parliaments and governments. If the agreements are implemented consistently, TURKPA could strengthen its role in aligning legislative approaches, advancing regional transport initiatives and expanding digital cooperation. If member states are unable to ensure the implementation of the adopted decisions, the Assembly’s activities may continue to focus primarily on political dialogue and the exchange of experience.
For Kyrgyzstan, the chairmanship offers an opportunity to combine parliamentary diplomacy with an economic agenda and advance initiatives that serve the interests of several countries. For Azerbaijan, it provides an additional channel for strengthening ties with Central Asia and promoting interregional cooperation. Ultimately, the significance of the new chairmanship will depend on whether political support and shared priorities can be translated into concrete cooperation mechanisms, new projects, and sustainable economic ties among Turkic countries.

ST. PETERSBURG/KYIV — Russia is ready to resume trilateral talks with the United States and Ukraine in mid-November, focusing on establishing a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends, according to the Kremlin.
Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Moscow's readiness to US special envoy Steve Witkoff during their three-hour meeting in St. Petersburg earlier in the day, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters on Wednesday.
Ushakov said the possibility of resuming trilateral negotiations was specifically discussed at the meeting. He added that Putin briefed Witkoff on the situation along the line of contact in Ukraine, while Witkoff informed Putin about the recent talks in Oslo, Norway.
The two sides also discussed the possibility of implementing large-scale economic projects between Russia and the US, some of which are approaching the implementation stage, Ushakov added.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he would agree to a peace deal with Russia that would freeze the conflict along the current frontline, the Interfax-Ukraine news agency reported on Wednesday.
"Right now, we need to freeze the situation. I believe this is a realistic way to put an end to this war," Zelensky said.
He added that following a potential ceasefire, Ukraine would seek security guarantees from Trump and European countries.
"The most important thing is peace, and peace supported by security," he said.
On Tuesday, Zelensky discussed proposals for various ceasefire formats with Witkoff in Oslo.
